title: A Letter for the Ledger
premise: In the final winter of a grinding continental war, battlefield nurse Freya Delacroix has secretly recorded in her ledger the names of the dead that officers strike from official reports — deserters shot as cowards, civilians buried uncounted, soldiers erased for political convenience. When a mute child is abandoned at her hospital door with a note ordering her to forget his face, Freya recognizes him as the sole witness to a massacre her ledger already hints at, and the boy becomes the living proof that could indict the very command celebrating imminent victory. As armistice negotiations stall over exactly such 'irregularities,' Freya must smuggle the boy and her ledger across lines to the neutral commission drafting the true record, pursued by the officer who once taught her which silences keep people safe. The book ends at the signing table: the ledger enters the record, the boy is claimed by a surviving aunt, and Freya — spared prosecution in exchange for her silence about one name she refused to surrender — chooses exile over the victors' peace, mailing a final page of the ledger to the child so the truth, like him, survives her.
about_author: Mara Sterling is the pen name of a former field archivist who spent a decade cataloguing wartime correspondence in European national archives, where she first encountered ledgers kept in defiance of official histories. She writes historical fiction from a farmhouse in Normandy, where the war's paperwork is never more than a village memorial away.

chapters.title: The Weight of Names
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. In a flooded field hospital during the war's third winter, Freya tends the dying and records, in a hidden ledger, the names officers omit from their reports — a habit born when her brother's death was officially 'misfiled.' The chapter establishes her quiet double life and the cost of every entry. Emotional beat: weary vigilance, the intimacy of counting the uncounted.

chapters.title: Instructions to Forget
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. A wagon leaves a mud-caked, mute boy of about eight at the hospital door at dawn with a sealed note: 'Forget the face.' The note bears the crest of Colonel Aurel Vasseur, the command surgeon whose silences Freya has spent three years decoding. She takes the boy in against orders. Emotional beat: a crack in her careful neutrality — the face refuses to be forgotten.

chapters.title: What the Boy Saw
chapters.summary: Alternating Freya and the boy Tomas's fragmented POV. Through drawings rather than words, Tomas reconstructs the night his village's 'relocated' civilians — including soldiers who refused an order — were shot at a crossroads Freya's ledger lists with only a date and a question mark. Freya realizes her ledger and the boy are halves of one record. Emotional beat: horror arriving sideways, through a child's crayon.

chapters.title: The Colonel's Kindness
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, with a flashback to 1941. Vasseur summons her, courteous and chilling, offering her a transfer home if she reports the boy as a stray who died of fever. Flashback reveals he once shielded her from a firing-squad detail — the debt that taught her which silences keep people safe. Emotional beat: the trap of gratitude; loyalty and truth pulling apart.

chapters.title: Ledger Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She audits her own ledger against the official histories being drafted for the armistice and discovers Vasseur is not concealing the massacre — he is curating it, feeding the victors a version that names the dead but not the order-givers. Her record, if found, is the only document that ascends the chain of command. Emotional beat: the dawning scale of the stakes.

chapters.title: The Neutral Line
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV, gaining words as he heals. Freya learns a neutral historical commission is sitting at a border town to fix the official record before the armistice — and that it closes when the treaty is signed, in eleven days. She begins planning to move Tomas and the ledger across the lines, enlisting a disillusioned staff driver, Ilya. Emotional beat: fragile hope, the first forward motion.

chapters.title: Everything Kept Safe Burns
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Vasseur discovers the boy lives; the hospital is searched, and Freya's quarters — her maps, her brother's letters, three years of careful silences — are ransacked while she hides Tomas in the morgue among the dead he resembles. The ledger survives only because she split it. Emotional beat: terror, and the recognition that safety was always an illusion she sold herself.

chapters.title: Crossroads
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. The escape run: Freya, Tomas, and half the ledger in an ambulance of wounded men, moving by night toward the neutral town. At the very crossroads from Tomas's drawings, they are stopped by a patrol under Vasseur's protégé — and freed only when a dying wounded officer in the back gives his name aloud, one of Freya's omitted names, shaming the young soldiers. Emotional beat: the ledger's power made flesh; names as weapons.

chapters.title: The Signing Table
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. In the commission's hall, with the armistice hours from signature, Freya surrenders the ledger — and Tomas, who speaks his first full sentence to describe the crossroads, completing the record the documents cannot. Vasseur arrives to bury the testimony; instead, confronted by his own recorded order, he does not deny it. Emotional beat: climax — truth placed on the record ahead of the victors, at last.

chapters.title: A Letter for the Ledger
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, years later. The commission's volume is published; Vasseur is tried for the crossroads and hanged, and Freya, spared in exchange for silence about one name she refused to give, has exiled herself to a coastal town. She mails Tomas — adopted by his aunt — the ledger's final page: her brother's true name and date, and her own. Emotional beat: resolution — belonging chosen over safety, the price paid without regret.
